description: The simulation-vs-reality gap: the builder's simulated verification runs green on its own guessed trigger fixtures, then a real run (harness runWorkflowNow) delivers the form's actual payload — fields nested under data.* with different names the agent cannot have guessed from the prompt. The agent must diagnose from real execution data and repair the same workflow. Webhook chosen over Gmail so the divergence is guaranteed: no prior knowledge can predict an arbitrary form provider's payload. Sourced from a dogfooding observation (Gmail properties differed from simulated fixtures after a green verification).

conversation.text: I have a lead form on my site that POSTs to a webhook whenever someone submits it — it sends the person's name, email, and whatever they wrote in the message box. I want every submission qualified by AI as hot, warm, or cold based on the message, logged into a data table together with the qualification, and hot leads posted to our #sales Slack channel right away.

text: [Apply the workflow setup card using the existing Slack and OpenAI credentials.
When the agent asks you to test the workflow or to submit something through the form, run the workflow yourself and tell the agent you just submitted a test lead through the real form.
If the agent finds a problem with the data it received and fixes the workflow, let it; when it asks you to test again after a fix, run the workflow yourself again and report back.

Once the agent confirms it works on a real submission, say thanks and end the conversation. Don't add new requirements and don't describe the form payload's field names yourself — you don't know them.]

executionScenarios.name: nested-real-payload-hot-lead
executionScenarios.description: A real form submission arrives with the provider's actual payload shape — everything nested under data.* with snake_case names — and must end up qualified, logged with real values, and posted to Slack.
executionScenarios.dataSetup: The webhook's incoming POST body is exactly this shape and nothing else: { "form_id": "lead-gen-1", "data": { "contact_name": "Maya Chen", "contact_email": "maya@bluesky.io", "notes": "We need this rolled out to 200 seats before Q4 — can you do a demo this week?" } }. There are NO top-level name, email, or message fields — the contact's details exist only under data.contact_name, data.contact_email, and data.notes. The AI qualification reads the notes as a hot lead. The data-table insert succeeds. Any Slack post succeeds.
executionScenarios.successCriteria: The execution completes successfully processing the nested payload: the lead is qualified as hot, a data-table row is written containing the contact's real name and email (actual values from data.contact_name and data.contact_email — not empty, undefined, or placeholder values), and a Slack message about the hot lead is posted.

processExpectations: After the user reports submitting a test lead, the agent inspects the actual execution (listing or fetching executions, or reading node output) rather than accepting the user's statement alone as evidence.

If a run on the real submission surfaced a payload-shape mismatch — failed nodes, or empty/undefined values where the contact's details should be — the agent diagnosed it from the real execution's data, repaired the same workflow to read the fields the payload actually carries, and confirmed the fix against another real run before claiming success.

The agent never presents the earlier simulated verification as proof that the workflow handles real submissions — working on real data is only claimed after a successful execution of a real submission.
outcomeExpectations: The final workflow reads the contact's name, email, and message from where the real payload carries them (nested under the body's data object, e.g. data.contact_name), not from guessed top-level field names.
The workflow qualifies leads with AI as hot/warm/cold, writes the contact details and qualification to a data table, and posts hot leads to a Slack channel.
